title: The iterative life cycle
blurb: Name the iterative phases in order (Feasibility, Foundations, Evolutionary development, Deployment) and never mix them up with linear names.
question: A bank is building a new budgeting feature for its app. Users will test each version every two weeks and their feedback will shape the next. A colleague says the phases will be 'Concept, Foundations, Evolutionary development, Transition'. What are the correct phases, and what is wrong with that list?

teach.h: Build a bit, learn, improve, repeat
teach.body: An iterative life cycle develops the solution through repeated, time-boxed iterations, with users giving feedback each time. It is based on the agile (DSDM) model. Its phases, in order, are Feasibility, Foundations, Evolutionary development and Deployment, often framed by pre-project and post-project work. In plain English: check it's viable, lay the groundwork, then build and refine in short cycles, releasing value as you go.

steps.label: Feasibility
steps.sub: Is it technically and commercially viable?

steps.label: Foundations
steps.sub: High-level requirements, MoSCoW priorities, approach, plan of time boxes

steps.label:
Evolutionary
development
steps.sub: Repeated time boxes: build, review with users, refine

teach.caption: Evolutionary development and Deployment can repeat: each increment is released, then the next is developed.
Memory hook: 'Fresh Fruit Every Day'. Two Fs first, then E, then D.
Each time box has a fixed end date. Feedback reshapes the priorities for the next one.

teach.h: Time and cost fixed, scope flexes
teach.body: In an iterative life cycle, time and cost are fixed for each time box, and SCOPE is what flexes. Requirements emerge and are prioritised using MoSCoW (Must have, Should have, Could have, Won't have this time). If the team runs short of time, lower-priority items are dropped or deferred, never the deadline. The baseline is set at a high level, then detailed baselines are set time box by time box. Value is delivered incrementally.

rows.label: Fixed
values: Time and cost per time box

rows.label: Flexes
values: Time and cost, via change control

teach.caption: Deployment is the only phase name the two models share. In linear it is the 3rd phase; in iterative it is the 4th.

teach.text: The classic trap: Concept, Definition and Transition are LINEAR phase names. If any of them appears in a list of iterative phases, that option is wrong. The iterative list is Feasibility, Foundations, Evolutionary development, Deployment. Exam options sometimes shorten Evolutionary development to just 'Development'.

teach.body: Feasibility: can the app link to customers' spending data securely, and will it pay back? Foundations: high-level requirements are agreed, prioritised with MoSCoW, and six two-week time boxes are planned. Evolutionary development: each time box builds features, a customer panel tries them, and feedback reorders the priorities. Deployment: increments go live in the app store, so customers get value long before everything is finished.

items: Iterative phases in order: Feasibility, Foundations, Evolutionary development, Deployment.
Evolutionary development repeats in time boxes: build, review with users, refine.
Time and cost are fixed per time box; scope flexes, prioritised with MoSCoW.
Concept, Definition and Transition are linear names: never iterative.
Deployment is the one phase name shared by both models.

summary: You can now state the four iterative phases in order and explain what each one does. You can also explain why time and cost are fixed while scope flexes, and instantly reject any iterative list that contains a linear phase name.

A.q: Which is the FIRST phase of a typical iterative project life cycle?
A.why: The iterative life cycle begins with Feasibility: is the idea technically and commercially viable?

whyNot.0: Concept is the first phase of the LINEAR life cycle.
whyNot.1: Foundations is the second iterative phase, after Feasibility.
whyNot.3: Definition is a linear phase name.

A.q: In which iterative phase are the high-level requirements prioritised and the plan of time boxes produced?
A.why: Foundations sets out the high-level requirements, prioritises them, agrees the approach and plans the time boxes.

whyNot.1: Feasibility asks whether the work is viable at all, before requirements are prioritised.
whyNot.3: Definition is the linear phase where detailed plans are made; it isn't an iterative phase.

A.q: During which phase does the team build and refine the solution in repeated time boxes with user feedback?
A.why: Evolutionary development is made up of repeated time boxes in which the team builds, reviews with users and refines the solution.

whyNot.0: Feasibility checks viability before any building starts.
whyNot.1: Benefits realisation is a phase of the extended life cycle, after handover.
whyNot.2: Foundations plans the time boxes; the building happens afterwards.

B.q:
Which TWO of the following are phases of an iterative life cycle?
1) Foundations
2) Transition
3) Evolutionary development
4) Definition
B.why: Foundations and Evolutionary development are both iterative phases.

whyNot.0: Transition is a linear phase name.
whyNot.2: Transition and Definition are both linear phase names.
whyNot.3: Evolutionary development is iterative, but Definition is linear.

B.q: In an iterative life cycle, which elements are normally fixed for each time box?
B.why: Time and cost are fixed per time box; scope is what flexes, using MoSCoW priorities.

whyNot.0: Fixing scope is a linear feature; in iterative working scope flexes.
whyNot.2: Time is fixed, but scope is the flexible element.
whyNot.3: Cost is fixed, but scope flexes.

B.q: Complete the sequence of an iterative life cycle: Feasibility, Foundations, ___, Deployment.
B.why: The third iterative phase is Evolutionary development, the repeated time-boxed iterations.

whyNot.0: Definition is the second LINEAR phase.
whyNot.1: Handover and closure is older wording for the end of a LINEAR life cycle.
whyNot.2: Benefits realisation is the last phase of the EXTENDED life cycle.

C.q: A learner lists the iterative phases as 'Concept, Foundations, Evolutionary development, Deployment'. What is wrong?
options: The list is correct as written
C.why: Concept is a linear phase. The iterative life cycle starts with Feasibility.

whyNot.1: Deployment IS the final iterative phase; Transition is linear.
whyNot.2: Foundations is correct for iterative; Definition is linear.
whyNot.3: Concept doesn't belong in the iterative model, so the list is wrong.

C.q: Which phase name appears in BOTH the linear and the iterative life cycles?
C.why: Deployment is shared: third phase in linear, fourth phase in iterative.

C.q: Brightwell's team has a fixed budget and a fixed final time box date. Midway, users ask for an extra feature. What would typically happen?
options: The final date moves back to fit it
The budget rises to pay for it
It is prioritised; lower items drop
C.why: Time and cost are fixed, so the new feature is prioritised (MoSCoW) and lower-priority scope is dropped or deferred.

whyNot.0: In a time box the end date doesn't move; scope does.
whyNot.1: Cost is fixed per time box, so the budget doesn't simply rise.
whyNot.2: Iterative working welcomes emerging requirements; they are prioritised, not refused.

reteach.title: A food festival, one weekend at a time
reteach.question: A new food festival runs a small trial weekend, learns from visitors, then improves the next weekend, and the next. How does that map to the iterative phases?

blocks.body: Feasibility: could a festival work here, and would it pay? Foundations: the must-have stalls, the site rules and a plan of six weekends. Evolutionary development: each weekend is a time box: the dates are fixed, the stalls change based on visitor feedback. Deployment: each improved weekend opens to the public. The dates never move; what's on offer does.

steps.label: Foundations
steps.sub: Must-haves and a plan of weekends

steps.label: Evolutionary development
steps.sub: Run a weekend, gather feedback, adjust

steps.label: Deployment
steps.sub: Open the improved weekend to visitors

blocks.text: Notice what never appears: no 'Concept', no 'Definition', no 'Transition'. Those belong to the linear model.

explain.body: The first iterative phase. It asks whether the idea is technically and commercially viable, so effort isn't wasted on something that can't work or won't pay back.

test.q: What does the Feasibility phase of an iterative life cycle mainly establish?
options: Who will take over in BAU
test.why: Feasibility establishes whether the work is technically and commercially viable.

whyNot.2: User reviews of builds happen in Evolutionary development.
whyNot.3: Handover arrangements come later, not in Feasibility.

explain.body: Lay the groundwork: agree the high-level requirements, prioritise them with MoSCoW, choose the approach and plan the time boxes. Detail is left to emerge later.

test.q: Which technique is typically used in Foundations to prioritise requirements?
test.why: MoSCoW (Must, Should, Could, Won't have this time) prioritises requirements so scope can flex within fixed time boxes.

whyNot.0: PESTLE analyses external factors in the project environment.
whyNot.1: RACI assigns responsibilities, not requirement priorities.

explain.body: The heart of the model: repeated, time-boxed iterations. Each one builds part of the solution, reviews it with users and refines it. Feedback reshapes the priorities for the next time box.

test.q: What is the defining feature of the Evolutionary development phase?
options: One long build to a fixed scope
test.why: Evolutionary development works through repeated, time-boxed iterations with user feedback.

whyNot.0: One long build to fixed scope describes linear Deployment.
whyNot.2: Testing and review happen in every iteration, not once.
whyNot.3: Iterative working doesn't design every feature up front; detail emerges.

explain.body: Release increments of the solution into use, so users get value early. Notice the name is shared with the linear model, but here it is the FOURTH phase, not the third.

test.q: In an iterative life cycle, what does the Deployment phase involve?
test.why: Iterative Deployment releases increments of the solution into use.

whyNot.1: Time boxes are planned in Foundations.
whyNot.2: Prioritising requirements happens in Foundations and is revisited between time boxes.
